claim: The Bay of Bengal makes more of the north Indian Ocean's cyclones than the Arabian Sea in every period checked, but its share has fallen from about three in four (76%, 1982-2003) to about two in three (66%, 2004-2024).

evidence.quote: CS+: Bay(BB+MM)=63 Arabian=20 ratio=3.15 Bay share=76%
CS+: Bay(BB+MM)=59 Arabian=30 ratio=1.97 Bay share=66%

method: Count of IBTrACS v04r01 NI main tracks with IMD (NEWDELHI) winds, seasons 1982-2024; genesis sub-basin = sub-basin of first IMD fix (BB = Bay incl. Andaman Sea; AS = Arabian Sea; MM = IBTrACS 'missing' sub-basin, used by one storm only, Gay 1989, whose first IMD fix is in the Gulf of Thailand, western Pacific basin, near 7N 105E; Gay is counted as Bay by choice because it matured and made landfall in the Bay, and without it Bay CS+ is 121, ratio 2.42, share 71%, SCS+ 62%, so no headline number changes); peak = max NEWDELHI_WIND; IMD classes CS>=34 kt, SCS>=48, VSCS>=64, ESCS>=90, SuCS>=120. Script method/count_ibtracs.py; output method/count_ibtracs_output.txt.

claim: Over IMD's whole record (1891-2024), the Bay had almost four times as many cyclones as the Arabian Sea (536 vs 139), but a smaller share of them turned severe (46% vs 62%).

evidence.quote: 1891-2024 (134 yrs): disturbances Bay 1246 Arabian 253 | cyclones Bay 536 Arabian 139 ratio 3.86 | severe Bay 244 Arabian 86 ratio 2.84 | severe share of cyclones Bay 46% Arabian 62%

method: Sum of IMD annualcd.pdf columns CYCLONES and SEVERE CYCLONES by basin; script method/count_imd_annual.py.
notes: IMD's own table (data owner). Early-period counts (pre-satellite) are less reliable, especially for weaker open-sea storms, which may lower the Bay's 'severe share'; that is why the 1982-2024 window is the spine (C001, C003). Both point the same way.
